answer: Let the mechanism define dynamic opportunity-cost bonds $\mathcal{B}$ where the payoff $\Pi$ for $n$ identities is $\Pi(n) = \frac{R}{n} - \mathcal{B}(n)$, ensuring $\frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial n} < 0$. By mapping penalties to a subgame-perfect punishment matrix, any Sybil attack becomes an island of loss, a canyon of negative expected utility. At dawn of the game, the cost of identity multiplication exceeds potential rewards, forcing convergence to a strict Nash equilibrium.
